header.title: Kaiserchronik A (V) (Vorau, Stiftsbibl., Cod. 276): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:rem:anonymous:m121y:norm, from the Referenzkorpus Mittelhochdeutsch, ReM 2.1 (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Referenzkorpus Mittelhochdeutsch, ReM 2.1 and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.14170: The original has Etzel for Attila and Ovene (Ofen) for Buda. 'Vulcânû' taken as Vulcano, the volcanic island.
notes.12177: 12177: 'ir' may be 'you' or 'her'; the sense depends on what precedes. 12183: 'dâse' read as 'dâ se', 'them there'. 12184: 'hornblâse', literally 'horn-blower', a term of abuse of unclear force.
notes.170: 170-171: these lines finish a passage begun before the unit, and their sense depends on it; 'an dem sameztage sâ' is literally 'at once on the Saturday'.
notes.3513: 3516 wîlsælde: the fortune fixed by the hour (of birth or death), the old man's word for fate under the stars; rendered 'the fortune of the hour'. 3536 zehenzic tûsent read as 'a hundred thousand'.
notes.4205: 4234 warten is read as worten, 'words'; it could instead be 'guards' or 'watch'.
notes.13855: Etzel is the German name of Attila.

nodes.text: for which they had no love.
straightway, on the Saturday.
One is called the Rotunda;
that was a splendid temple.
The god was called Saturn;
after him it was to the honour of all devils.
Whenever the Romans
had prayed in there
as they wished,
they hurried out to the field.
Very great was their revelry,
with tourneying and with leaping,
with dancing and with singing.
Whoever then won more
praise and honour,
he was all the better off.
The book tells us
that the good St Boniface
later consecrated that same house,
a very holy lord,
to the honour of almighty God,
and after him of St Mary
and all God's saints.
When the very holy man
came to the throne in Rome —
he was the fourth pope after St Gregory —
he was in great anxiety
that the impurity should remain beside him.
Then the holy man sent
for all the good Christians
whom he knew of anywhere in Rome.
They put on wool and went barefoot;
his gathering became very large.
He went foremost to the door;
at once he began to consecrate.
He wedded the house to the true God.
The devils burst out through the top,
some into the abyss.
Of this there is evidence in Rome to this day.
Now we must take up again
where we left the story.
Now follow him no more."
Then both the brothers said,
"Master, he has killed an unblemished child
and has buried it under his bed;
with it he works whatever magic he wants.
His wonders are so many:
he says, if we will follow him,
we shall turn lead into gold;
he says, if anyone tries to seize him,
that one can never come near him;
whenever he wants to hide himself,
no one can see him;
whenever he wants to die
and come alive again,
whenever it pleases him,
then he is in hell;
whenever he wants, in heaven,
Then he answered him thus,
the holy apostle:
"Now choose from the crowd
twelve of the wisest;
let us go home to your house;
take your dead one out of there,
an unblemished child,
with which you have worked magic;
you have buried it under your bed.
There we shall have an end of this dispute."
God's adversary
was sorely frightened at these words;
Then the old man said:
“Dear [son], I can tell you all this better
than you could understand it yourself.
The fortune of the hour must always come to pass.
You are still a young child.
There are twenty-four hours
in the day and in the night;
each of them has its power.
They become neither more nor fewer;
they never change at all;
they are all of equal length.
Son, take this into your mind:
how could a person, by his skills,
hold back their course among them?
Pythagoras proved this for you: the
hour that was a thousand years ago,
If you will labour after it,
you will still find it ready.
Truly I tell you this:
had you applied yourself a little better,
astronomy would be well known to you.
You say also that old and young
have come to a battle;
now suppose a hundred thousand have lost their lives:
whoever lay dead there,
that was his hour and his day;
he could not escape it,
whatever death he was to die.
Whether he drowns or is slain,
the hour must carry him to it,
just as it stands within it.
All this is governed by the seven planets,
which rule the heavens
and compose the hours,
and each of them separately
rolls all the way round
and must go through its time.
Of that you can tell me nothing;
I was brought up in the books.
then have us put to torment,
however it pleases you.”
On the third day, very early,
the country people gathered from all sides,
knights and ladies;
they were eager to see the wonders —
a very great host of the Romans.
Simon the conjurer came there too.
He climbed up on a bronze pillar;
all the people bowed to him.
The devils carried him up into the air
with great strength.
Saint Paul fell to the ground;
he prayed sweetly and worthily.
Saint Peter stood upright.
Both were ready for martyrdom.
With heart and with mind
they reminded the good God
of what he had promised his disciples
when he left them in great sorrow:
whatever they asked in his name,
he would do it all;
that he should not let the devil
bring shame on Christendom.
When the lords had prayed as they ought,
they did as they wished.
Saint Peter raised his hand;
he made manifest my Lord's power.
He said, “I command you, black devils,
by the words of almighty God,
in the name of the holy Christ,
that you hold him up no longer:
let him fall back down,
as a sign to all these people
that God alone reigns
over all this world together,
over earth and over sea
and over all the heavenly host.”
As Saint Peter completed the cross,
the devils fled at once from the spot.
They let go of the conjurer;
they hurled him to the ground.
He fell so that he burst apart entirely.
How sad the emperor became then!
Then King Nero grew angry.
No human being dared come near it
unless he wanted to fetch his death there.
There went the Hebrew man;
he bade the bull stand still.
It was all done.
He bade them draw back from him,
both poor and rich.
He let no one hear it;
he whispered into its ear.
As soon as he had finished a word,
the bull fell down dead.
Then all together rejoiced,
the Jews and the heathens.
Now hear, all of you together,
how I settle the dispute for you:
if Zambri has done it with God,
then let him also, with God, bid him rise up again.
If he cannot accomplish that,
then no one need praise his works.
and you would lose my lord's favour.
Truly, he did not know what he was about.
That same witch —
he ought never to tolerate her at his court.
In anger he went into the hall;
there the maidens were sitting all around.
He said, "Why are you guarding them there,
you wicked horn-blower?
It would be more fitting for you to go off to the woods
than to look after the maidens here.
You are a witch,
and you sit here hung with gold."
She said, "God knows, sir, good fellow,
you do me great wrong,
for I offered you my service
so that you would leave me in peace.
God knows well the truth of it,
whether I am a witch
or ever practised any sorcery."
He meant to strike her a blow,
to kick her with his foot;
in honour of the holy faith.
That displeased the young lords.
Then God arranged it thus,
that the one brother, Astrolabius,
and the other, his companion,
if he would put his hope for it in God.
Now the book tells us thus:
that the priest, lord Eusebius,
while he was a youth,
had read in the black books;
he had applied himself to them
so that he was well versed [in them].
When the devil had lured him so far away,
no one else could undo it,
unless he got back his ring,
unless my Lord alone should do it.
One morning, very early,
he took the youth with him;
he then read in a book;
it was not long
before the devil came there.
He conjured him so earnestly
that he put the matter to him:
who had brought it about
that harm befell the child,
and whether he had a hand in it.
Then the devil answered him thus:
"*Sim*, lord Eusebius,
you swore an oath before
that you would keep your Christian faith;
now you are forsworn.
Truly, I was never in such distress,
for, God knows, to me
it was never so hot in hell
as it is for me near you.
Now give me a respite in this matter,
allow me to go away from here;
I will deal with it as you wish."
Then the servant of God said,
"I command you under God's ban
to bring me the ring;
there can be no other way.
Hurry off very quickly;
within half a while
his dear sons.
Then it came about soon after
that Etzel drowned in his own blood.
Dietmar, the good hero,
rode into the land at Meran.
Very many saw this:
that the devils took him.
They carried him into the mountain at Vulcano;
St John, the holy man, commanded them to.
There he burns until the Last Day,
and no one can help him.
Whoever now wants to prove
that Dietrich saw Attila,
let him have the book brought out.
When King Attila was buried at Buda,
after that, it was, in truth,
forty-three years
before Dietrich was born.
He was brought up among the Greeks;
there he girded on the sword.
